[EMERGING] Tests find bugs. Proofs rule them out. 🔐

Google DeepMind says its new AlphaProof Code framework let AI agents write machine-checked proofs of security properties for Signal's protocol code. Human experts chose what to prove; the agents did the proving, and humans reviewed about 1% of the codebase. The company says the verification took about four weeks.

As a test, the team reintroduced two previously fixed bugs. In both cases the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.

Reality check: these are company-reported results. A proof is only as strong as the properties it states, so independent review of the scope matters.

Sources (link in bio):

2:
[EMERGING] Is AI speeding up AI research? Check the speedometer, not the odometer.

The odometer tells you how far AI has come. The speedometer asks whether progress itself is getting faster. Independent evaluator METR tried to read that dial for one lab: it estimates Anthropic is improving model capabilities on well-specified tasks about 1.9x faster than it did between March 2024 and October 2025.

Reality check: METR says it would not be surprised if the true figure were closer to 1.3x or 3x. Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR found most informative, and benchmark gains may not map cleanly to real-world impact. METR says it took no payment but received free tokens for the work.

Sources (link in bio):
METR, Nov 5, 2026: "Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026" (metr.org/blog)

[IMAGINE] What if AI training worked hardest when the sun is high and the wind blows? ☀️

AI data centers are becoming big new electricity users, and grids are already stretched: three major US grids set record demand peaks this summer. Today most big computing jobs run whenever they are scheduled.

Imagine instead that long training runs could pause at grid peaks and speed up when solar and wind are plentiful, turning data centers into flexible helpers rather than only new loads. Caveat: live services can't wait, and shifting work across time and places is hard. This is speculation, not a product.

Which AI jobs could wait for clean power? Tell us in the comments.

4:
[EMERGING] Can a quantum computer grow by plugging chips together? IBM is betting on it.

IBM says clients and partners have run 34 billion circuits on its 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 processor, reporting speedups of up to 19x compared with earlier work on its older Heron chips. The next version, r3, is designed for 10,000 operations on 520 programmable qubits. In 2027, IBM plans to link two of them into a single 1,040-qubit system.

Reality check: the speedups are partner-reported and measured against IBM's own previous hardware, not against the best classical computers. The 520-qubit chip and the 2027 system are plans. IBM's chip-to-chip links reached 99.3% transfer fidelity, short of its 99.9% target.

Sources (link in bio):
IBM Newsroom, Nov 11, 2026: "IBM Quantum Nighthawk demonstrates new levels of speed and quality" (newsroom.ibm.com)

5:
[EMERGING] Quantum algorithms are recipes, and Toffoli gates are the costly steps.

On future error-corrected quantum computers, some operations are cheap and some, like the Toffoli gate, are slow and expensive to produce. Cutting their number is like rewriting a recipe so it needs fewer hours in the oven.

In a new preprint, researchers from Harvard, QuEra and Anthropic had large language models propose circuit designs while an independent automated checker verified and scored them. For one decoder, a key step in a quantum optimization method, the Toffoli count fell from about 5.1 million to about 440,000.

Reality check: these are resource estimates for individual building blocks, not runs on real hardware, and the paper is a preprint.

[IMAGINE] What if the power grid had a quantum co-pilot? ⚡

Running a grid is a giant juggling act: solar and wind rise and fall, batteries charge and discharge, and more cars plug in every year. Energy companies are already testing quantum machine learning on grid optimization problems, with early results reported on IBM hardware.

Picture a future where quantum processors help with the hardest planning puzzles, working alongside the classical computers that run grids today rather than replacing them. That is speculation: today's results are experiments, not grid operations.

What should a quantum co-pilot tackle first? Tell us in the comments.

[TODAY] Three of America's biggest power grids broke all-time demand records this summer.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Texas's ERCOT grid hit 91.1 GW on July 22, 2026, 6.5% above its previous record from August 2024. PJM, which serves much of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, reached 162.6 GW on July 2, and SWPP in the central US hit 58.0 GW on July 27.

Why it matters: grids are built for their highest hour, not their average day, so new peaks drive investment in power plants, storage and transmission.

Caveat: EIA's figures come from hourly data reported by each grid operator and may differ slightly from the operators' own published numbers.

[TODAY] Think of a grid battery as a lunchbox for sunshine: pack it at noon, open it at dinner. 🔋

Solar panels produce the most power around midday, but demand often peaks in the evening. Grid batteries bridge that gap by storing cheap midday electricity and releasing it when people get home.

That lunchbox is getting cheaper. Ember's Global Electricity Review 2026 reports that battery costs fell a further 45% in 2025, while deployment grew 46% to an estimated 250 GWh worldwide.

Reality check: most grid batteries are built to cover hours, not days or seasons, so long windless winter stretches still need other solutions.

[IMAGINE] What if a fusion power plant could rehearse every startup in software before it ever runs for real?

That idea has a real starting point. According to the American Nuclear Society's newswire, the US Department of Energy selected Commonwealth Fusion Systems to lead a project building an AI-enabled digital twin of SPARC, its prototype fusion device being assembled in Massachusetts.

Imagine operators practicing on a virtual machine, testing risky settings safely and learning before the real plasma ever forms. Reality check: SPARC is still a prototype, fusion electricity is not on the grid yet, and a digital twin is only as good as the physics behind it.

What would you test first? Tell us in the comments.
